correctness.rationale: Normalized covariance yields exactly K(S,T)=n(n−1)(|S∩T|−k²/n)/[k(n−k)]. A one-step hypergeometric telescoping identity proves the finite norm formula. At k≪√n the expectation bound yields zero normalized limit; at k~c√n factorial moments and uniform integrability give the Poisson profile; at k≫√n a four-cell Stirling expansion with every cell→∞ gives the central mass and Gaussian endpoint limit. The Poisson profile peaks at each mean m+1/2; the exact convergent negative even-power series for successive logarithmic peak ratios proves global unique maximum at mean 1/2. Compactness of rank ratios gives every-maximizer localization. A self-contained exact checker confirmed 1979 rational (n,k) tests and exact small projection idempotence; these tests are not a universal proof.

originality.rationale: Claimed originality is limited to the all-ranks sharp limit √(2/e), its strictly sparse maximizing rank k/√n→1/√2, and the complete three-scale Poisson/Gaussian crossover. The exact hypergeometric mean absolute deviation reduction is admitted as published. The inspected first-harmonic decomposition and finite homogeneous-space papers do not optimize endpoint norms over slice rank. The closest public second-Johnson projector theorem explicitly treats degree two, not degree one. The 2026 hypergeometric-mean-deviation manuscript is only abstract-accessible; its abstract treats fixed proportional margins and Poisson mean tending to infinity, not the root-rank global optimization. That comparison is limited, not represented as full-text exclusion.
residual_risks: Full primary text of arXiv:2608.06232 could contain a joint-margin optimization not indicated by its abstract. It was not falsely classified as non-covering from snippets.

value.rationale: The global endpoint amplification across all Johnson slice ranks is a natural operator-stability quantity not determined by fixing a rank or a density. The sharp universal coefficient √(2/e) and forced sparse rank k~√(n/2) distinguish a genuinely Poisson extremal regime from the seemingly natural dense-rank Gaussian regime √(2/π). The new parameter localization and three-scale classification give structural scope beyond a one-point absolute-deviation identity. The proof does not claim exact finite optimal ranks, convergence rates or higher-degree projectors.
